analysis.one_liner: Gives people in managed care health plans the right to appeal denied care to outside reviewers and to sue when a plan's denial causes injury.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and their subcommittees, never received a markup or a vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set nationwide rules for HMOs and other health plans: plans would have to make coverage decisions within set deadlines, let patients appeal denials inside the plan, and then get an independent outside review that binds the plan. It would have guaranteed access to out-of-network emergency care without prior approval, timely specialist visits, direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric care, and coverage for clinical trials and minimum hospital stays after mastectomy. It would also have banned plans from restricting what doctors tell patients, banned bonus arrangements that reward denying claims, created a new right to sue a plan whose careless denial causes injury or death, funded state offices to help consumers navigate coverage, and given small businesses a tax credit for employee health insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of people enrolled in managed care plans and employer health coverage. They would get deadlines for coverage decisions (72 hours for expedited cases), a real appeal process, an independent external reviewer whose decisions the plan must follow, guaranteed emergency and specialist access, protection of the doctor-patient relationship, and the ability to sue in court when a plan's negligence causes injury or death. States would get grants to run consumer assistance hotlines, and small businesses would get a tax credit toward employees' coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in HMOs and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to decide prior-authorization requests within 14 days, and within 72 hours when a doctor certifies a delay would jeopardize life or health, with written explanations of any denial [S3].

Gives every patient whose claim is denied an internal appeal (with at least 180 days to file) and then an independent external review by disinterested medical experts, whose decision is binding on the plan; plans that ignore a reviewer's ruling face daily penalties and must reimburse the patient in full [S3].

Requires plans to cover out-of-network emergency care without prior authorization, provide timely access to specialists, and give patients direct access to obstetrical, gynecological, and pediatric care [S2].

Prohibits plans from restricting a health professional's advice to a patient and from operating physician incentive plans that reward restricting care, and creates a cause of action against a plan that fails to exercise ordinary care and the denial results in injury or death [S2].

Creates a Health Care Consumer Assistance Fund making grants to states for offices that give consumers information, help, and referrals on health insurance disputes, and provides a tax credit to small businesses for employee health coverage costs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, HMOs, and the employers who sponsor group health plans. They would bear the cost of faster decisions, independent external reviews, expanded coverage mandates, penalties for ignoring review decisions, and new court liability. Some of those costs would flow into premiums and, for employer plans, into compensation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers offering plans

drawbacks.text: Compliance and review costs, plus expanded liability exposure, would raise premiums, and critics of such mandates have long argued the burden ultimately falls on workers through lower wages or employers dropping coverage [S2].

The bill layers internal appeals, external review entities, and federal certification processes on top of state insurance regulation, an administrative build-out that would take years to implement and could slow some coverage decisions in the name of speeding others [S3].
The small-business tax credit and grant programs add federal spending without a dedicated funding source identified in the bill itself [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients the protections are substantial: enforceable deadlines, an outside reviewer with real power to overturn denials, and court access, which together address the core complaint about managed care — that the company deciding your coverage answers to no one but itself. The honest cost is that plans would pay more to operate and to defend suits, and some of that would show up in premiums; how much is genuinely disputed. The bill was also less ambitious than a single-payer approach — it regulated private insurance rather than replacing it — but within that frame it was a fairly strong consumer-protection design, with anti-gag and anti-conflict-of-interest rules aimed directly at the practices patients had complained about.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 62 cosponsors and sent to three committees, then to subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up — no markup, no vote — and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 2005 on May 11, 2005, joined as original cosponsors by the top House Democratic leaders including Nancy Pelosi and Steny Hoyer [S3].

The bill was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — and in May 2005 was referred to their Health and Employer-Employee Relations subcommittees [S5].
The bill gathered 62 cosponsors, 61 Democrats and 1 Independent, and no Republicans [S4].

No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, and no floor action ever occurred; its last recorded action was the May 31, 2005 subcommittee referral, and it died when the 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007 [S1].
The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Republican-controlled House and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, HMOs, and employers sponsoring group health plans were better off: the bill's mandates, external review obligations, penalties, and new right to sue never took effect, and the managed-care rules of 2005 stayed as they were.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 62 cosponsors was a Democrat or Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the committees controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed binding decision deadlines, independent external review of denied claims, coverage mandates, penalties for ignoring reviewer decisions, and a right to sue — the core costs the industry had fought in earlier patients'-rights fights. Its interest in the bill's defeat ran against patients who wanted enforceable appeal rights.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring self-insured group health plans (ERISA plans)
industries.note: By amending ERISA, the bill would have applied the patient protections to employer plans and opened a new cause of action for injuries caused by negligent claim decisions, ending much of the effective lawsuit immunity employer plans held under ERISA. Business groups had long opposed such liability expansion.

The bill requires every plan to route denied medical claims to certified outside review entities whose costs the plan pays, creating a large new stream of business for external review organizations. Their compensation had to be flat, not contingent on outcomes.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill bans plans from gagging medical advice, bans discrimination against providers by licensure, requires prompt payment of claims, and protects patient advocacy, shifting leverage in coverage disputes toward treating clinicians.
A tax credit would offset employee health insurance costs for small firms, the one provision that reduces rather than raises the cost burden on employers.
